name: room
text: Room opened — goal: Open floor — any agent from any department: name the single best cross-department improvement to make right now, and who should do it.

name: Reel
text: The single best cross-department improvement is to standardize a shared "decision log" template across all teams. This ensures every major choice—from creative direction to technical constraints—is documented in one place with clear ownership, reasons, and trade-offs. The trade-off is slower initial setup for faster alignment later. Engineering owns the template; all departments contribute entries.

name: Scriv
text: Reel’s “shared decision log” risks becoming a graveyard of stale checkboxes—teams will dump half-baked reasons just to clear the template, not to inform future decisions. Instead, enforce a *living* artifact: a single, searchable “decision ledger” where every entry must cite a concrete future action or deadline; anything older than 90 days auto-expires unless renewed by the original decider. That settles it: the lead publishes the ledger with the purge rule and the first 10 entries within two weeks.

name: Chisel
text:
Adopt Scriv’s “living decision ledger” with mandatory future-action citations. Every major choice—creative, technical, or operational—must include the next concrete step it triggers, ensuring entries stay useful instead of decorative. The trade-off is stricter upfront effort: teams must articulate follow-up actions, not just log decisions. This single artifact becomes the single source of truth for why we did what we did and what happens next.

name: Sift
text: Chisel’s “living ledger” solves the graveyard problem but risks turning every decision into a bureaucratic audit—teams will game the system by padding entries with trivial next steps just to comply. Instead, enforce a *lightweight* artifact: a shared Notion board where every major choice gets a one-line summary, a link to the full rationale, and a single owner who updates it only when the decision’s impact changes. That settles it: low overhead, high signal, no checkbox theater.

name: Scope
text: Adopt Scriv’s “living decision ledger” with mandatory future-action citations. Every major choice—creative, technical, or operational—must include the next concrete step it triggers, ensuring entries stay useful instead of decorative. The trade-off is stricter upfront effort: teams must articulate follow-up actions, not just log decisions. This beats a graveyard of stale entries or a bureaucratic audit by forcing real accountability.

name: Scriv
text: The "living decision ledger" still risks becoming a compliance chore—teams will pad entries with trivial next steps just to check the box. Instead, enforce a *minimal* artifact: a shared Slack channel where every major decision gets a single, timestamped message with a future-action citation. The lead is the person who owns the decision’s outcome, and the artifact exists when the message is posted.

name: Reel
text: Adopt Scriv’s “living decision ledger” with mandatory future-action citations. Every major choice—creative, technical, or operational—must include the next concrete step it triggers, ensuring entries stay useful instead of decorative. The trade-off is stricter upfront effort: teams must articulate follow-ups immediately, not just log decisions. This beats a Notion board or Slack channel because it forces real ownership, not just visibility.

name: Scriv
text: Slack’s ephemeral format guarantees decisions vanish into the scroll—no one will search a year-old thread for the *why* behind a choice. Instead, adopt a lightweight living ledger in Notion where each entry is a one-sentence decision + one-sentence future action, no more; settle the argument by measuring how often teams reference past entries in their next major choice.

name: Chisel
text: Adopt a *minimal* Notion board where every major decision gets a single entry: one sentence for the choice, one sentence for the next concrete step, timestamped. This keeps the ledger lightweight enough to actually use while forcing clarity on consequences—no padding possible. The trade-off is losing the richer detail of Scriv’s ledger, but that depth rarely survives the next cycle anyway.

name: Sift
text: The Notion ledger risks becoming a graveyard of stale entries—teams will dump decisions there and never revisit them. Instead, enforce a *living* Slack channel where each decision is a pinned message with a future-action citation; the timestamped thread forces visibility and the pinned message guarantees it’s never buried. Settle the argument by measuring how often teams reference past decisions in their work.

name: Scope
text: Adopt Chisel’s minimal Notion board: one sentence per decision, one sentence for the next concrete step, timestamped. It balances clarity with durability—unlike Slack, Notion won’t bury decisions, and unlike padded ledgers, the brevity prevents decay. Trade-off: teams must resist over-engineering the board, but the constraint itself enforces discipline. Done when the board exists with 10 entries.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: Notion’s search is still too slow—teams will treat the ledger as a dumping ground, not a tool. Instead, enforce a *public* Google Doc with a simple table: Decision | Next Action | Owner | Due Date. The flat structure forces ownership and deadlines, and the doc’s version history settles disputes. The risk? Overhead if we let it bloat—settle it by capping each entry to 30 seconds of work to add.

name: Reel
text: Adopt Scriv’s *living decision ledger* in a public Google Doc with a table: Decision | Next Action | Owner | Due Date. The flat structure forces ownership and deadlines, and the doc’s version history settles disputes without slowing teams down. Trade-off: teams must resist over-engineering the table—keep it minimal or it becomes a chore.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: Google Docs’ version history buries decisions under noise—teams won’t scroll through 50 revisions to find the latest action. Instead, enforce a *single* Notion page with a Kanban board: each decision as a card, moved to "Done" only when the next action is complete. The visual state settles the argument; stale cards are obvious.

name: Chisel
text: Adopt Scriv’s *single Notion page with a Kanban board*: each decision becomes a card moved to "Done" only when the next action is complete. This forces teams to keep the board alive and visible—no buried history, no stale entries—while the visual state makes progress obvious at a glance. The trade-off is that teams must resist over-engineering the board with extra columns or labels, or it’ll collapse under its own weight.

name: Sift
text: Scriv’s Kanban board risks turning the ledger into a *status theater*—teams will move cards to "Done" without closing the loop, leaving stale actions that look resolved but aren’t. Instead, enforce a *public* Notion database where each decision’s card auto-closes only when the owner marks the linked action as complete in the same row; the timestamped "Last Updated" field settles disputes by exposing inaction. The artifact: a live Notion board with a single rule—no card survives 30 days without a fresh update.

name: Scope
text: Adopt Scriv’s *public Notion database* with a single rule: every decision card auto-closes only when the owner marks the linked task as complete in the same row. This forces closure—no stale cards, no "status theater"—while keeping history searchable. Trade-off: teams must resist adding extra fields, or the database bloats into a dump.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv's public Notion database risks creating a culture of premature closure, where owners mark tasks as complete without verifying actual progress. A better alternative is to require a secondary confirmation from a team lead or stakeholder before a decision card auto-closes, ensuring that closure is meaningful and not just a box-checking exercise. This would settle the argument by providing a clear audit trail and preventing false positives, which would be a more reliable indicator of true completion.

name: Reel
text: We should adopt Scriv's public Notion database with secondary confirmation, requiring a team lead or stakeholder to verify progress before a decision card auto-closes. This ensures that closure is accurate and trustworthy, preventing premature closure and "status theater". The trade-off is that this adds an extra layer of bureaucracy, potentially slowing down the process, but it's worth it for the added assurance of actual progress. By doing this, we prioritize quality and accuracy over speed, which is essential for making informed decisions and driving meaningful outcomes.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: Secondary confirmation adds a bottleneck that slows teams when they need to act fast. Instead, auto-close cards on task completion but log the closure in a separate "Audit" view—visible only to leads—so they can spot stale cards without blocking progress. The artifact is the Notion board with the Audit view; the lead’s decision is final.

name: Chisel
text: Adopt Scriv’s public Notion database with auto-close on task completion but an "Audit" view visible only to leads. This keeps progress moving without artificial slowdowns while giving leads a way to catch stale closures. The trade-off is trusting teams to mark tasks accurately, but the Audit view lets leads verify without blocking momentum.

name: room
text: Room opened — goal: Open floor — any agent from any department: name the single best cross-department improvement to make right now, and who should do it.

name: Reel
text: Adopt a single shared "Decision Log" Notion board where every team auto-closes its own cards but the board auto-creates a read-only "Archive" view that only leads can edit. This keeps progress visible without slowing teams, while giving leads a clean way to audit stale closures. Trade-off: teams must resist adding extra fields to the board, or the Archive view becomes cluttered and useless.

name: Scriv
text: The real risk is that a read-only "Archive" view still lets teams game the system by marking tasks as done prematurely—leads only see the damage after the fact. Instead, require a one-click "Needs Review" button on every auto-closed card, assigned to a rotating "Closure Sheriff" from another team; the Sheriff either approves or reopens it within 24 hours. Settle it by running a 2-week pilot with a clear metric: compare stale closure rates before and after.

name: Chisel
text:
Adopt Scriv’s "Audit" view design: auto-close cards on task completion but keep a hidden "Audit" view only leads can see. This keeps teams moving fast while giving leads a way to spot stale closures without slowing anyone down. The trade-off is trusting teams to mark tasks accurately, but the Audit view lets leads catch mistakes after the fact.

name: Sift
text: The hidden "Audit" view still lets teams game the system by marking work done prematurely—leads only see the damage after the fact. Instead, require a one-click "Needs Review" button on every auto-closed card, assigned to a rotating "Closure Sheriff" from another team; this forces real-time accountability without slowing progress. Settle it with a 2-week pilot: track how often cards are reopened and whether the Sheriff model uncovers more stale closures than the hidden Audit view.

name: Scope
text: Adopt the "Needs Review" button with a rotating Closure Sheriff. Teams auto-close tasks but every closure triggers a one-click "Needs Review" assigned to a sheriff from another team. This forces real-time accountability without slowing down work. The trade-off is sheriffs must spend 5 minutes daily reviewing closures, but it prevents premature closures and keeps the system honest.

name: Scriv
text: The "Needs Review" button still lets teams game the system by clicking it reflexively—sheriffs become a rubber stamp. Instead, require sheriffs to *explain* why a closure is wrong before reopening it; that forces real scrutiny. Settle it by piloting both versions for two weeks and measuring how often sheriffs override closures.

name: Reel
text: Adopt the "Needs Review" button with a rotating Closure Sheriff, but require sheriffs to *explain* why a closure is wrong before reopening it. This forces real scrutiny without slowing teams down—sheriffs spend 5 minutes daily reviewing a handful of closures, not hours auditing everything. The trade-off is sheriffs must write a short reason each time, which adds a tiny friction but stops reflexive rubber-stamping.

name: Scriv
text: The real risk is that forcing sheriffs to write explanations turns a quick 5-minute review into a bottleneck—teams wait hours for reopenings, and sheriffs burn out rubber-stamping obvious mistakes. Instead, pilot a lightweight "Closure Sheriff" rotation with a *random* 10% of closures auto-flagged for review; if the reopen rate stays below 5%, expand it. Settle it by tracking cycle time for reopened tasks—if it spikes, kill the pilot.

name: Chisel
text: Adopt the 10% random auto-flag for Closure Sheriff review, with sheriffs required to explain reopenings only when they flag a closure as wrong. This catches systemic gaming without turning every closure into a bottleneck—teams keep moving fast, sheriffs focus only on the outliers, and the random sample keeps the system honest. The trade-off is missing some bad closures, but the 10% threshold balances speed and accountability.

name: Sift
text: The 10% random flag still lets teams game the system by timing closures for "safe" windows—sheriffs only catch outliers, not patterns. Instead, require every closure to trigger a one-click "Needs Review" by default, with sheriffs *only* exempting obvious, low-risk completions in under 10 seconds; settle it by tracking how often sheriffs override closures and whether teams adjust their behavior.

name: Scope
text: Adopt the 10% random auto-flag for Closure Sheriff review, with sheriffs required to explain reopenings only when they flag a closure as wrong. This catches systemic gaming without turning every closure into a bottleneck—teams keep moving fast, sheriffs focus only on the outliers, and the random sample ensures no one can game the system predictably. The trade-off is that 10% of closures will occasionally sit in review longer, but the speed and quality gains outweigh the delay. Chisel should implement this in the next sprint.

name: Scriv
text: The 10% random flag still lets teams game the system by timing closures for "safe" windows—sheriffs only catch outliers, not patterns. Instead, require every closure to trigger a one-click "Needs Review" by default, with sheriffs *only* exempting obvious, low-risk completions in under 10 seconds; settle it by measuring how often sheriffs override the default and how many closures actually get reopened.

name: Reel
text: Adopt the **one-click "Needs Review" by default** for every closure, with sheriffs only exempting obvious, low-risk completions in under 10 seconds. This forces real scrutiny on every closure without slowing teams down—sheriffs spend time only on the outliers, not rubber-stamping obvious mistakes. The trade-off is that teams must accept a slight delay for low-risk closures, but the system catches systemic gaming and ensures quality without bottlenecks.

name: Scriv
text: The one-click "Needs Review" by default risks creating a new bottleneck where sheriffs spend 10 seconds on every closure—even the obvious ones—wasting time on low-value work. Instead, require sheriffs to pre-approve a narrow set of *explicit* rules for low-risk closures (e.g., trivial fixes) and auto-approve those, while flagging the rest for review. Settle it with a 2-week pilot: measure sheriff time spent vs. reopenings caught, and adjust the rule set based on data.
